meta.title: Melas, urs and festivals of Pakistan
notes: Part 1 (melas) has 41 curated entries across Pakistan with history, timing and what happens. Part 2 (auqaf_urs_calendar) is the Punjab Auqaf Department's urs/event calendar as the page showed it.

This is not every mela in Pakistan. Thousands of small local melas and urs are never listed online. Sindh, KP, Balochistan, Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Kashmir are thin because only Punjab publishes an official urs calendar I could read.

The Auqaf page said about 245 events but only 212 rows could be read, so Part 2 is probably incomplete. Dates are exactly as published: they mix Islamic months (Safar, Rajab), Punjabi/desi months (Haar, Sawan, Bhadon, Katak, Chet, Jeth, Assu) and Gregorian months, and the page has apparent typos (reversed ranges like '19 - 18 Shaban'). Names are also as published, including misspellings.
Auqaf entries are grouped by Auqaf zone, not city. A zone can cover several districts, so no city is claimed. The Auqaf page also gave no shrine addresses.
Islamic-calendar dates move about 11 days earlier each year, so no 2027 dates are given. Check with the relevant Auqaf department or local press before publishing dates.
Where sources disagree on a date, both are shown and noted.
latitude/longitude are null (no source gave coordinates). Use google_maps_url or geocode the venue.

Images: image_* fields are empty. Run fetch_images.py on your own computer to find freely licensed Wikimedia Commons photos, convert them to WebP and fill image_credit_line. I could not download images from my workspace, so the script is untested against live Wikimedia, though its logic was tested with mock data. Review image_review.csv before publishing.
verified=false means not confirmed by a phone call or visit. Melas and urs can be cancelled or moved for security or weather.

melas.name: Mela Chiraghan (Mela Shalimar, Festival of Lights)
melas.venue: Shrine of Shah Hussain (Madho Lal Hussain), Baghbanpura, next to Shalimar Gardens
melas.when_held: Last weekend / last week of March per Punjab Auqaf and a travel site; the 2025 edition ran 11-14 April
melas.history: Marks the urs of the Punjabi Sufi poet Shah Hussain (1538-1599). It was once held inside Shalimar Gardens; Ayub Khan ordered it moved out in 1958. Ranjit Singh is said to have led a procession from Lahore Fort to the site in the early 19th century.
melas.what_happens: Lighting of oil lamps and candles, qawwali, Heer recitals, talks on Shah Hussain, Punjabi poetry, folk food and sweets, a handicrafts bazaar.
melas.status_notes: Daily Times reported it 'returned after 67 years' in April 2025, organised by the Walled City of Lahore Authority at Shalimar Gardens and the shrine. Wikipedia describes it in the present tense. The shrine's urs likely continued; the large public mela was the part that was revived. The sources do not say why it stopped.
image_queries: Shrine of Madho Lal Hussain Lahore

melas.name: Urs of Data Ganj Bakhsh (Ali Hujwiri)
melas.when_held: 18-20 Safar (Punjab Auqaf); one source says 19 Safar. The date moves each year with the Islamic calendar (24 August in 2024).
melas.history: Urs of the 11th-century Sufi Ali Hujwiri, who died in Lahore around 1072 CE. His shrine is described as the most visited in the city. The 2023 edition was called the 980th urs and the 2024 edition the 981st.
melas.what_happens: Mahfil-e-Sama (devotional music), Quran recitation, lectures on Sufism, and free langar food distribution.
melas.status_notes: 2024 dates were announced by the Punjab Auqaf Secretary.

melas.name: Urs of Baba Farid Ganj Shakar
melas.when_held: Muharram (about the first 10 days)
melas.duration: About 10 days while the Bahishti Darwaza stays open
melas.history: Urs of the 13th-century Sufi saint. Wikipedia's festival article reports up to 0.9 million visitors in 2016.
melas.what_happens: The Bahishti Darwaza (Gate of Paradise) is opened for pilgrims to pass through, with devotional gatherings.
melas.status_notes: The Punjab Auqaf calendar lists 5 Muharram for Chilla Gah Baba Farid in Lahore and '29-30 Haar' for the Pakpattan shrine itself, so check the exact dates with Auqaf before publishing.

melas.name: Urs of Hazrat Lal Shahbaz Qalandar
melas.when_held: Moves with the Islamic calendar; 17-19 February in 2025 (the 773rd urs)
melas.history: Annual urs of the Sufi saint Syed Muhammad Usman, known as Lal Shahbaz Qalandar (died 1274 per Wikipedia).
melas.what_happens: A floral chadar is laid by the Sindh Governor at the start and by the Chief Minister at the end; Shahbaz Awards; the Malakhra cultural competition; Sindhi cultural programmes; literary conferences; handicraft exhibitions; folk music. Jamshoro district gets a public holiday on the first day and Sindh a provincial holiday on the last day.
melas.status_notes: 2025 had 5,000+ police and 32 medical camps. Section 144 banned bathing in nearby canals.

melas.name: Urs of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai
melas.venue: Shrine of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai; Shah Jo Bagh cultural village; HT Sorley Hall
melas.when_held: Moves with the Islamic calendar; 9-11 August in 2025 (the 282nd urs)
melas.history: Annual urs of the Sindhi Sufi poet, held at his shrine at Bhit Shah.
melas.what_happens: A floral chaddar and fateha at the opening, mystic and folk music, a cultural village with handicraft stalls, the Sugharan Ji Kachehri (his verses sung and discussed), and distribution of clothes and gifts to the needy.
melas.status_notes: Start date for 2025 is inferred from an article published 10 August 2025.
image_queries: Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai shrine Bhit Shah

melas.name: Sakhi Sarwar Urs / Sang Mela (Baisakhi fair)
melas.venue: Shrine of Sakhi Sarwar (Syed Ahmad Sultan), village of Muqam in the Sulaiman Mountains
melas.address: About 35 km from Dera Ghazi Khan city
melas.when_held: Around Vaisakhi, March-April; the Punjab Auqaf calendar lists 15 February to 15 May for this shrine
melas.duration: Wikipedia's festival article says week-long; Auqaf's longer range suggests pilgrim traffic over months
melas.history: Auqaf says the tomb was built in the 13th century and was expanded by Babur. Locally the fair is called Sang Mela and is celebrated for centuries.
melas.what_happens: Large pilgrim gatherings and a fair at the shrine.
melas.status_notes: Durations differ between sources; confirm locally.

melas.name: Urs of Waris Shah / Heer Ranjha Mela
melas.when_held: 9-11 Sawan (Wikipedia); about September (travel site); 9 Sawan in the Auqaf calendar
melas.history: Urs of Waris Shah, author of the Punjabi love epic Heer. Wikipedia says the Punjab government later decided to hold it in September.
melas.what_happens: Heer Ranjha reenactments and cultural performances, per one travel site.
melas.status_notes: Dates differ between sources.
image_queries: Waris Shah shrine Jandiala Sher Khan

melas.name: Urs of Baba Bulleh Shah
melas.when_held: August or September per a travel site; the Auqaf calendar lists 10-12 Bhadon
melas.history: Urs of the Sufi poet Bulleh Shah.
melas.what_happens: Qawwali, langar and devotional gatherings, per the travel source.
melas.status_notes: Single secondary source for activities.

melas.name: Urs of Hazrat Bahauddin Zakariya
melas.when_held: 27 Safar per Wikipedia; 5-7 Safar per the Punjab Auqaf calendar
melas.history: Urs of the 12th-13th century Suhrawardi saint.
melas.what_happens: Devotional gatherings at the shrine.
melas.status_notes: Dates conflict between sources; confirm with Auqaf.

melas.name: Urs of Hazrat Shah Rukn-e-Alam
melas.when_held: 5-7 Jamadi-ul-Awal per the Punjab Auqaf calendar; a travel site says July or August
melas.history: Urs of the 14th-century saint whose tomb is also on Pakistan's UNESCO tentative list.
melas.what_happens: Qawwali, langar and devotional gatherings, per the travel source.
melas.status_notes: Dates conflict between sources.

melas.name: Urs of Sultan Bahu
melas.when_held: September or October per one travel site
melas.history: Urs of the Sufi poet Sultan Bahu.
melas.what_happens: Qawwali, langar and devotional gatherings, per the travel source.
melas.status_notes: Only one secondary source; not in the Auqaf extract I could read.

melas.name: Urs of Hazrat Mian Mir
melas.when_held: 7-8 Rabi-ul-Awal (Auqaf calendar)
melas.history: Mian Mir died in 1635 at age 88 after living in Lahore for sixty years. Wikipedia's festival article also mentions extra rainy-season fairs at the mausoleum.
melas.what_happens: Devotional gatherings and fairs.

melas.name: National Horse and Cattle Show (Lahore)
melas.venue: Fortress Stadium and other Lahore venues (in 2025 also Lahore Fort, Minar-e-Pakistan, Lahore Polo Club, Bagh-e-Jinnah, Expo Center)
melas.when_held: February (9-23 February in 2025); other sources say February or March
melas.history: Began in 1964 at Fortress Stadium in the Ayub Khan era and has been held intermittently since.
melas.what_happens: Tent pegging, mounted archery, livestock competitions, a float parade, flower exhibition, kabaddi, Rustam-e-Punjab wrestling, vintage cars, a Sufi festival, children's festival and an industries and artisans expo. Wikipedia also lists polo and dog races.
melas.status_notes: Organised by the Punjab Parks and Horticulture Authority in 2025. Held intermittently, so check each year.

melas.name: Sibi Mela
melas.when_held: Wikipedia says the first fair was in January 1885; a blog says spring. Check current dates.
melas.duration: About a week (the 1887 fair ran 19-25 January)
melas.history: Started in 1885 as a horse show and grew into a cultural festival. Muhammad Ali Jinnah attended the 1948 gathering and addressed tribal leaders.
melas.what_happens: Animal markets, camel racing, tent pegging, handicraft and tribal dress exhibitions, folk dances; the 2018 edition added a livestock market, stalls and a music show.
melas.status_notes: Wikipedia flags the article as needing an update (December 2018).

melas.name: Shandur Polo Festival
melas.venue: Shandur Polo Ground, about 3,700 m, called the world's highest polo ground
melas.when_held: 7-9 July every year
melas.history: Started in 1930 by Colonel Evelyn Hey Cobb, per Wikipedia.
melas.what_happens: Freestyle polo between Chitral and Gilgit-Baltistan teams, folk music, dancing, traditional performances and a camping village.
melas.status_notes: Run jointly by the KP and Gilgit-Baltistan governments.

melas.name: Kalam Summer Festival (Kalam Mela)
melas.when_held: July or August
melas.history: First held in 2010 to promote tourism after peace returned to Swat. About 0.5 million tourists came in 2012.
melas.what_happens: Paragliding, jeep rally, cycling, canoeing, handicraft displays, music concerts and traditional dances.
melas.status_notes: Listed as active 2010 to present.

melas.name: Chilam Joshi (Kalash spring festival)
melas.when_held: Spring, from about 13 May. The KP Tourism Authority announced the 2024 edition in mid-May 2024
melas.history: A 2024 report calls it the oldest festival of the Kalash people. It marks the arrival of spring and is linked to preparations for new crops.
melas.what_happens: Music, dance, embroidered clothing, and a well-known ritual of dancing with walnut branches. Tourism police provided security and visitor guidance.
melas.status_notes: Valley names in the venue field are my addition and are not in the cited sources.

melas.name: Uchal (Kalash summer / harvest festival)
melas.when_held: From about 20 August; one source says August to September
melas.history: Harvest thanksgiving of the Kalasha people.
melas.what_happens: Feasts, a procession to a plateau, worship and night dancing.

melas.name: Choimus (Kalash winter festival)
melas.when_held: From about 15 December
melas.history: Winter festival of the Kalasha people. One blog claims UNESCO recognises it as intangible heritage; I could not confirm that.
melas.what_happens: Rituals, prayers, dancing and cedar burning; young people choose marriage partners per one source.
melas.status_notes: UNESCO claim unconfirmed.

melas.name: Basant (kite festival)
melas.venue: Rooftops, Walled City and Old Lahore
melas.when_held: Phaggan, late February or early February. The 2026 edition ran 6-8 February
melas.history: Spring festival of kite flying and yellow colours. It was banned in 2007 after deaths and injuries from sharp kite strings and celebratory gunfire. The Punjab government lifted the ban in 2025 through the Punjab Kite Flying Ordinance and Basant returned to Lahore in February 2026, about 18 years later. One Punjab minister's post said 25 years, which conflicts with Dawn's 18.
melas.what_happens: Kite flying from rooftops, yellow clothes and food, music, parties and fairs. 2026 rules allowed only thread-based string, set kite-flying zones under surveillance, and required motorbike safety wires or antennas.
melas.status_notes: Gulf News reported on 25 Feb 2026 that the Punjab home department told the Lahore High Court at least 17 people died during the 2026 festival (12 falls from roofs, 3 electrocutions, 2 falls from trees) and that more than 100 accidents were reported. The court is still examining the rules, and no source says whether Basant will continue in future years. Older web pages that say kite flying is banned are out of date.

melas.name: Baisakhi (Vaisakhi) fairs
melas.city: Lahore, Eminabad, Faisalabad, Dera Ghazi Khan; Nankana Sahib and Hasan Abdal (Sikh pilgrims)
melas.when_held: 13 or 14 April
melas.history: Marks the start of wheat harvesting. Wikipedia says Dera Ghazi Khan's cattle and camel trade is larger than India's Pushkar fair.
melas.what_happens: Bhangra, giddha, animal races and fairs; especially significant for Sikh pilgrims.
melas.status_notes: Wikipedia mentions a Lok Mela in Islamabad in 2017.

melas.name: Jashn-e-Baharan (spring / flower festival)
melas.venue: Race Course Park (Jilani Park) and other public spaces
melas.when_held: February-March
melas.history: Celebrates the start of spring.
melas.what_happens: Flower shows, handicrafts, live music, food stalls and family events.

melas.name: Lok Virsa Folk Festival (Lok Mela)
melas.when_held: October, per one tour site
melas.history: Described as Pakistan's largest cultural event.
melas.what_happens: Folk artists from many countries and provincial pavilions.
melas.status_notes: One source only; I did not check this year's dates. Venue name is my assumption from the festival name.

melas.name: Lohri
melas.when_held: 13 January (Poh)
melas.history: Marks the end of the coldest days of winter.
melas.what_happens: Bonfires, folk songs, sesame seeds, jaggery and nuts.

melas.name: Punjabi Culture Day
melas.when_held: 14 March
melas.history: Honours Punjabi arts figures.
melas.what_happens: Music, dance, bhangra, plays, exhibitions, film and food stalls.

melas.name: Pakistan Flower Show
melas.when_held: 23-26 February in one entry; March in another
melas.history: Annual flower exhibition in Karachi.
melas.what_happens: Flower exhibition.
melas.status_notes: Wikipedia lists it twice with different dates.

melas.name: Silk Route Festival
melas.when_held: September
melas.history: Celebrates the historic trade routes.
melas.what_happens: Artisans, folk music, markets and polo.
melas.status_notes: Single blog source.

melas.name: Blossom Festival
melas.when_held: April
melas.history: Spring celebration when valleys bloom.
melas.what_happens: Not described.
melas.status_notes: Single blog source.

melas.name: Winter feast and sports festival (blog calls it 'Sevendays Winter Feast')
melas.when_held: January
melas.history: Winter event.
melas.what_happens: Ice hockey, skating, ice sculptures and cultural shows.
melas.status_notes: Single blog source and the name looks unusual; check before publishing.

melas.name: Nowruz
melas.when_held: Spring; 21 March per one site
melas.history: Persian New Year marking spring; one site says it is observed by Ismaili and Shia communities in Gilgit-Baltistan.
melas.what_happens: Ceremonies, feasts, traditional food, music, dance and family gatherings.
melas.status_notes: Two tourism-site sources, no official calendar.

melas.name: Sindhi Cultural Day
melas.when_held: First Sunday of December
melas.history: Celebrates Sindhi heritage.
melas.what_happens: Rallies, traditional music and dance, and dress such as ajrak.
melas.status_notes: Single blog source.

melas.name: Urs of Hazrat Sachal Sarmast
melas.venue: Shrine of Sachal Sarmast; events at Sachal Complex, Mehfil-e-Sama Hall, Manjhand Ground and Malakari Ground
melas.when_held: Moves with the Islamic calendar; 14-16 March in 2025 (the 204th urs); earlier editions were held in April (2022, 2023)
melas.history: Annual urs of the Sindhi Sufi poet Sachal Sarmast.
melas.what_happens: A chadar-laying ceremony opens it, followed by a musical conference, an award ceremony, an exhibition, a Malakari (wrestling) event, musical evenings and a closing literary conference. Run by the Sachal Sarmast Shrine Committee headed by the Deputy Commissioner.
melas.status_notes: Malakari is a traditional Sindhi wrestling; that gloss is my addition, not stated in the cited article.

melas.name: Huner Mela (Hunar Mela)
melas.when_held: Opened on Friday 15 May 2026 (inferred from an article dated 16 May 2026)
melas.history: Organised by the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Culture and Tourism Authority to connect craftspeople with wider audiences.
melas.what_happens: More than 40 stalls of handicrafts (wax painting, Hazara phulkari embroidery, Charsadda chappals), a prison-made products stall, women entrepreneurs, a children's play area, a traditional hujra setup, a Kalash pavilion, a photo exhibition of KP destinations and documentary screenings.
melas.status_notes: I found only the 2026 edition; I don't know if it is held every year.

melas.name: Ginani Festival
melas.venue: Villages in Hunza, Nagar and Yasin
melas.when_held: About 21 June (summer solstice); one site says June
melas.history: A centuries-old festival that marks the start of the wheat harvest and thanks the land for a good farming season. It is linked to the Ismaili communities of Hunza, Nagar and Yasin; rulers once joined elders in the ceremonies.
melas.what_happens: Prayers led by elders, folk dances and concerts, and communal meals from fresh harvest produce.
melas.status_notes: Two tourism-style sources, no official calendar.

melas.name: Hinglaj Mata Yatra (Hinglaj festival)
melas.venue: Hinglaj Mata Temple, Hingol National Park area
melas.address: Hinglaj Mata Temple, Lasbela District, Balochistan
melas.when_held: Annually in spring; 17-19 April in 2026
melas.history: The temple is on Pakistan's UNESCO tentative list as part of the Hingol Cultural Landscape. Dawn says it receives nearly one million visitors a year.
melas.what_happens: Hindu rituals at the shrine, thousands of pilgrims walking from Sindh (about 20 days for many), a 24-hour free langar run by the Shri Hinglaj Mata Welfare Mandli, free medical camps, and ration bags from PDMA.
melas.status_notes: About 300,000 pilgrims came in 2026 per Dawn, which a senator said was three times the previous year. Heavy security: army, Frontier Corps, police and Levies.

melas.name: Maha Shivaratri fair, Umerkot Shiv Mandir
melas.venue: Umerkot (Amarkot) Shiv Mandir, near Rana Jaageer Goth
melas.address: Near Rana Jaageer Goth, Umerkot District, Sindh
melas.when_held: Every year on Maha Shivaratri
melas.history: Legend says a herder saw a cow giving milk to a lingam. The present structure was built about a century ago, reportedly by a Muslim man. The page calls it possibly the oldest Hindu place of worship in Sindh.
melas.what_happens: Pilgrims from lower and upper Sindh stay for the multi-day festival. Expenses are covered by the All Hindu Panchayat of Umarkot.
melas.status_notes: The page says about 250,000 people attend.

melas.name: Baisakhi Mela, Gurdwara Panja Sahib
melas.when_held: April; in 2023 celebrations ran 12-21 April with the main event on 14 April
melas.duration: A four-day mela inside a wider 12-21 April period (2023)
melas.history: One of the main Sikh pilgrimages in Pakistan.
melas.what_happens: Religious rituals, Granth Sahib readings, prasad cooked and distributed, then travel to Lahore and Nankana Sahib on 15 April. The government arranged security and special trains.
melas.status_notes: 2023 report expected more than 10,000 pilgrims from India, Europe and America.

melas.name: Guru Nanak birthday mela (Gurpurab), Nankana Sahib
melas.when_held: November; 11-14 November in 2023
melas.history: Marks the birthday of Guru Nanak at his birthplace.
melas.what_happens: A decorated city, free food for pilgrims, a procession on day three, worship, and a fair with trade stalls, a circus and rides. Pilgrims come from the USA, Canada, India, Australia and other countries.
melas.status_notes: The source text was partly garbled, so confirm details with the Evacuee Trust Property Board or the Punjab tourism department.

melas.name: Urs of Hazrat Bari Imam
melas.when_held: Moves with the Islamic calendar; 15-17 August in 2024
melas.history: Annual urs of Shah Abdul Latif Kazmi (1617-1705 per Wikipedia).
melas.what_happens: Exceptional security arrangements, facilities for devotees from across Pakistan and abroad, and special arrangements for women.
melas.status_notes: The 2024 plan was approved by a committee chaired by the Deputy Prime Minister.

melas.name: Urs of Hazrat Abdullah Shah Ghazi
melas.venue: Shrine of Syed Abdullah Shah Ghazi, Clifton
melas.when_held: Moves with the Islamic calendar; 27-29 June in 2024 (the 1294th urs). A 2025 headline mentions a public holiday on 19 June
melas.history: Annual urs of Syed Abdullah Shah Ghazi at his shrine in Clifton (Wikipedia's shrine list gives his years as 720-773).
melas.what_happens: The Sindh Governor and Auqaf minister open it with a flower wreath. Planned events include a Mehfil-e-Sama, a Mehfil Na'at and a special Milad Mehfil for women.
melas.status_notes: The 2025 date comes from a search headline I did not open.

melas.name: Cheti Chand (Jhulelal Jayanti), Darya Lal Mandir
melas.venue: Darya Lal Sankat Mochan Mandir, near Custom House, Saddar
melas.address: Near Custom House, Saddar Town, Karachi
melas.when_held: Not stated in the pages I read
melas.history: The temple is said to be about 300 years old, was attacked in 1965 and 1992, and was renovated and reopened in December 2015. It is dedicated to Darya Lal (Jhulelal).
melas.what_happens: Not described in the source.
melas.status_notes: The page names Cheti Chand as the temple's festival but gives no date or mela details. Another Sindhi festival temple, Shri Varun Dev Mandir at Manora, also appeared in search but I did not open it.
